questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'She will come to the party _____ she finishes her assignment.'
questions.explanation: 'If' introduces a positive condition — 'she comes' only under the condition that she finishes. 'Unless' introduces a negative condition (= 'if not'). 'Although' = despite / even though. 'Because' = cause (answers 'why?'). Test the logic — here coming depends on finishing, so 'if'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the sentence with the correct correlative pair.

options.option_text: Neither he or his brother is here.
Neither he nor his brother is here.
Either he nor his brother is here.
Neither he and his brother is here.

questions.explanation: Fixed correlative pairs — 'neither…nor', 'either…or', 'not only…but also', 'both…and', 'whether…or'. Mixing them (neither…or, either…nor) is ungrammatical. Verb agreement — with 'neither A nor B', verb agrees with the noun closer to it — here 'his brother' (singular) → 'is'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'He ran fast, _____ he missed the bus.'
questions.explanation: The two clauses contrast — running fast should have let him catch the bus, yet he missed it. 'But' marks that contrast. 'And' — mere addition. 'So' — cause leading to result. 'Or' — alternative. Use 'but' / 'yet' / 'however' for contrast, 'and' / 'moreover' for addition, 'so' / 'therefore' for consequence.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Walk fast, _____ you will miss the train.'
questions.explanation: An imperative + 'or' states the negative consequence if the command is not obeyed — 'Walk fast, or (else) you will miss the train' = 'If you don't walk fast, you'll miss the train.' 'Unless' would need rephrasing of the first clause. 'And' would mean the walking itself causes the missing, which is wrong here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses 'no sooner … than'?

options.option_text: No sooner he arrived than the rain started.
No sooner had he arrived than the rain started.
No sooner he had arrived than the rain started.
No sooner he did arrive than the rain started.

questions.explanation: After 'No sooner' (and 'Hardly', 'Scarcely', 'Seldom') at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary is inverted to before the subject — 'No sooner HAD he arrived…'. The second clause uses 'than' (not 'when'). Pair — 'Hardly had he arrived when the rain started.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: '_____ he was very tired, he continued to work.'
questions.explanation: The two clauses are in contrast — being tired should stop work, yet he kept working. 'Although' / 'though' / 'even though' — introduce a contrasting subordinate clause. 'Because' / 'since' — cause (reason). 'So that' — purpose. Never pair 'although' with 'but' in formal writing — 'Although it was raining, he went out' (not '…, but he went out').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct sentence with 'not only … but also'.

options.option_text: She not only sings but also dance.
She not only sings but also dances.
She not only sing but also dances.
She not only sings but also dancing.

questions.explanation: 'Not only … but also' requires parallel structure on both sides. If 'sings' (verb + s) follows 'not only', then 'dances' (matching form) must follow 'but also'. Options A, C, D break parallelism with 'dance' / 'sing' / 'dancing'.
